Consider the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2 \times 2$ matrix. Let $\Phi(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $\Phi(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation $\Phi'(t) = A \, \Phi(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $\big[ \mathbf{a}, \: \mathbf{b} \big]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}.$*

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t)$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_2'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_2(t)$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1'(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2'(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) =  \big[ A \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: A \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \Phi(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that ![](images/03/036695dd1a6ae9a121d25cae37b1ba7be7e77502b99335391da8d1d8d04972be.svg).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L6}$ follows from line $\textrm{L5}$ by ![](images/27/27f914bbca34dfde3debdcf58eb5a2205eda059ceafa10bf6964bb7c6a984d1c.svg).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L7}$ follows from line $\textrm{L6}$ and substitution from line ![](images/b4/b48e9d724fed6566873ba6c844fcfa10c92fcd810012da503960972f8c4105c3.svg).
:question/worked-solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L2}.$ Since $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns $\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular,

$$
\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t).
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that $\mathbf{x}_1$ is a solution of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L5}$ and $\textrm{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
\Phi'(t)=\big[A\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:A\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big]
= A\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big].
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L5}$ by factoring out $A$ on the left.

:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+2\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t),$ denoted $\Phi_0(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
\Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \quad \Phi_0(0)  = I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -7{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1 = 7\textrm{i}t, \qquad
\lambda_2 = -7\textrm{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((7\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(7\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(7\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+7\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & =7\cdot \frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:
    

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=3 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}_{3} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}-(2)=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}+2=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}$ and ${x}_{3}=2$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}+(\frac{5}{2})-(2)=3\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3+2-\frac{5}{2}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{5}{2}$, ${x}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}$, and ${x}_{3}=2.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨\frac{5}{2},\frac{5}{2},2⟩.$

:question/problem:

Solve the following system of equations:
    

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=\frac{1}{2} \\ y+z &=1 \\ z &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that  $z=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get 

$$
y+2=1\,⟹\,y=1-2=-1.
$$

Now, we substitute $z=2$ and $y=-1$into the first equation to get

$$
x+(-1)+(2)=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}-2+1=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-\frac{1}{2}$, $y=-1$, and $z=2.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨-\frac{1}{2},-1,2⟩.$

:question/problem:

$$
:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that ${x}_{3}=3.$ Substitute this into the second equation to get

$$
{x}_{2}-(3)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-1+3=2.
$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{3}=3$ and ${x}_{2}=2$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-(2)+(3)=1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1-3+2=0.
$$

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=0$,  ${x}_{2}=2$, and ${x}_{3}=3.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨0,2,3⟩.$

he third equation states that  $z=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem:

:question/worked-solution:

$$
{x}_{2}+(-1)=-\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{1}{2}.

Now, we substitute ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${x}_{3}=-1$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-2(\frac{1}{2})+(-1)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+1+1=4.

$$
:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that $z=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$

$$

Now, we substitute both $z=2$ and $y=0$ into the first equation to get

$$

$$

$$
:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say,  ${x}_{1}$, ${x}_{2}$, and ${x}_{3}.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=5 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{3} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}+(2)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-2.
$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{3}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=-2$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-3(-2)+4(2)=5\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5-6-8=-9.
$$

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=-9$, ${x}_{2}=-2$, and ${x}_{3}=2.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨-9,-2,2⟩.$

{x}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-1-\frac{2}{3}=-\frac{5}{3}.

Now, we substitute ${x}_{3}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{3}$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}+3(-\frac{5}{3})+(2)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+5-2=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=5$, ${x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{3}$, and ${x}_{3}=2.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨5,-\frac{5}{3},2⟩.$

:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x$, $y$, and $z.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+3z &=-2 \\ y+4z &=0 \\ z &=3\end{aligned}\right.

$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{3}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=4$ into the first equation to get

:question/problem:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x$, $y$, and $z.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-1 \\ y+3z &=2 \\ z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that $z=3.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+3(3)=2\,⟹\,y=2-9=-7.

Now, we substitute $z=3$ and $y=-7$ into the first equation to get

$$
x+(-7)+2(3)=-1\,⟹\,x=-1+7-6=0.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=0$, $y=-7$, and $z=3.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨0,-7,3⟩.$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{3}=-3$ and ${x}_{2}=4$ into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}+2(4)+3(-3)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1-8+9=0.

 Substituting this into the second equation, we get

:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations represented by the augmented matrix: 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x$, $y$, and $z.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations: 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+z &=2 \\ 3y+2z &=-1 \\ -z &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that

$$
-z=2\,⟹\,z=-2.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
3y+2(-2)=-1\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{3}(-1+4)=1.
$$

Now, we substitute $z=-2$ and $y=1$ into the first equation to get

$$
x+(-2)=2\,⟹\,x=2+2=4.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=4$, $y=1$, and $z=-2.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as 
$$
\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x$, $y$, and $z.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y+z &=-1 \\ y+z &=1 \\ 2z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that
 

$$
2z=1\,⟹\,z=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(\frac{1}{2})=1\,⟹\,y=1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we substitute $z=y=\frac{1}{2}$  into the first equation to get

$$
2x+(\frac{1}{2})+(\frac{1}{2})=-1\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}(-1-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})=-1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-1$, $y=\frac{1}{2}$, and $z=\frac{1}{2}.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨-1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.$

:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations that is represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3\end{array} 
	\right].
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ 3{x}_{3} &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that

$$
3x_3=3 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
	x_3=1.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(1)=-2
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_2=-2-1=-3.
$$

Now, we substitute both $x_3 = 1$ and $x_2 = -3$ into the first equation to get

$$
2x_1+(-3)-(1) = 0
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} (3 + 1) = 2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x_1 = 2,$ $x_2=-3,$ and $x_3 = 1.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 2,-3,1 \rangle.$

:question/worked-solution:
For random variables ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n},$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}] & \text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}] & ⋯ & \text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{n}] \\ \text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{1}] & \text{Var}[{X}_{2}] & ⋯ & \text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{n}] \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \text{Cov}[{X}_{n},{X}_{1}] & \text{Cov}[{X}_{n},{X}_{2}] & ⋯ & \text{Var}[{X}_{n}]\end{aligned}].
$$

That is,

- the $i$th diagonal element is ${Σ}_{ii}=\text{Var}[{X}_{i}],$ and

- the element in the $i$th row and $j$th column for $i\ne j$ is ${Σ}_{ij}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].$

Now, note that

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{Cov}[Y,X].
$$

As a result, the covariance matrix is always symmetric (moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix). 

So, we can find the missing elements as follows:

- $a={Σ}_{12}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]=\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{1}]={Σ}_{21}=1$

- $b={Σ}_{23}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]=\text{Cov}[{X}_{3},{X}_{2}]={Σ}_{32}=1$

- $c={Σ}_{31}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{3},{X}_{1}]=\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]={Σ}_{13}=0$

Therefore, $a+b+c=1+1+0=2.$

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.1$ |

Given that $\text{E}[X]=2$ and $\text{E}[Y]=1.2,$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.1$ | $0.5$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.6$ | $0.4$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a support ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5-{2}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a support ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.6+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.4 \\  & =3.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =3.6-{1.2}^{2} \\  & =2.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =(1)(0)f(1,0)+(3)(0)f(3,0)+(1)(3)f(1,3)+(3)(3)f(3,3) \\  & =0\cdot 0.2+0\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.3+9\cdot 0.1 \\  & =1.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.8-2\cdot 1.2 \\  & =-0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -0.6 \\ -0.6 & 2.16\end{aligned}].
$$

If $E[X] = \frac{4}{3}$ and $E[Y] = \frac{8}{3}$, find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y$.

> A scientific calculator is required to answer this question.

The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}x+y,\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[Y]=\frac{7}{12},$ and $E[{X}^{2}]=\frac{5}{12},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}-{(\frac{7}{12})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}-{(\frac{7}{12})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}xy(x+y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-(\frac{7}{12})\cdot (\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{11}{144} & -\frac{1}{144} \\ -\frac{1}{144} & \frac{11}{144}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}11 & -1 \\ -1 & 11\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}48y(x-y),\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \frac{x}{2}, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{4}{5},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1}{4},$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{2}{3},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48{y}^{3}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}(x{y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{160}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{3}{320}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{20}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48x{y}^{2}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{24}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{5}{192}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{24}-(\frac{4}{5})\cdot (\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{120}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{75} & \frac{1}{120} \\ \frac{1}{120} & \frac{1}{80}\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\, & -1\le x\le 1,\,\,-1\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $\text{E}[X]=0$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{5}{4},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{4}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-{(0)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{33}{5} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}-{(\frac{5}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{51}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[-1,1]\times [-1,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{51}{80}\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{16}({x}^{2}-y),\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{3},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{20}{21},$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=\frac{40}{27},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$
We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{4}-y{x}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[y{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{[\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}-{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{Var}[Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{40}{27}-{(\frac{20}{21})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{760}{1\,323}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}xy({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}x]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}{x}^{7})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{7}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{[\frac{1}{8}{x}^{8}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-(\frac{5}{3})\cdot (\frac{20}{21}) \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{63} & \frac{5}{63} \\ \frac{5}{63} & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{aligned}].
$$

:question/problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3},\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $\text{E}[X]=\frac{2}{3}$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{8}{5},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$
:question/worked-solution:
For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-{(\frac{8}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[0,1]\times [0,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=2x$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{4}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=[\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{8}{75}\end{aligned}].
$$

How can we best describe the following matrix?

A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Notice that $A$ is a matrix for which all entries above the diagonal are $0$'s:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}

$$

:question/problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$*
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(-4+\text{i})t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}

﻿﻿﻿

$$

The characteristic equation is $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(3-\lambda )(6-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -3)(\lambda -6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$

**Note:** The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are always the entries on the main diagonal.

:question/problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

B-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}2-\lambda  & 5 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(B-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following:

$$

:question/problem:
$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -9 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -10 & 0 \\ -18 & 18 & -36 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ given above. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\lambda =-1$ is an eigenvalue of $P$

- **II.** $\lambda =-10$ is an eigenvalue of $P$

- **III.** The eigenvalue $\lambda =-10$ has algebraic multiplicity $3$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,P-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
P-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -9 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -18 & 18 & -36 & -4-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(P-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Notice that we can expand the $4\times 4$ determinant across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -9 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -18 & 18 & -36 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-10-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -18 & -36 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the $3\times 3$ determinant across the $2$nd row, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-10-\lambda )\cdot (-10-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -18 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-10-\lambda )^{2}((-1-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )-54) & =0 \\ (\lambda +10)^{2}({\lambda }^{2}+5\lambda -50) & =0 \\ (\lambda +10)^{2}(\lambda +10)(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ (\lambda +10)^{3}(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $P$ are $\lambda =-10$ (with algebraic multiplicity $3$) and $\lambda =5.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

- **II.** $\lambda =-4$ is an eigenvalue of $P$
- **III.** The eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$

﻿﻿﻿

$$
P-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}5-\lambda  & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & -\lambda  & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -4-\lambda  & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(P-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Notice that we can expand the $4\times 4$ determinant across the $1$st column, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & -\lambda  & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -4-\lambda  & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & 0 & 7 \\ -3 & -4-\lambda  & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the $3\times 3$ determinant across the $3$rd row, we obtain the following:

$$

$$

So, the eigenvalues of $P$ are $\lambda =5,$ $\lambda =2,$ $\lambda =0,$ and $\lambda =-4$  (all with algebraic multiplicity $1$).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

$$

$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & \le 4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})=4(1)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\le 4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =4(1)^{2}+3(0)^{2}+2(0)^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the maximum value of  $Q(x)$ is equal to $4.$

\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \ge 4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})=4(1)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\ge 4.$ 

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no smaller than $4.$ But before we conclude that $4$ is the minimum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=4.$

Notice that when  $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4(1)+7(0)^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the minimum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $4.$

Now, recall that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is equivalent to $x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 =1.$ So, 

$$

$$

and, in turn, $Q(\mathbf{x}) \geq -6.$

So, the value of $Q(\mathbf{x})$ can be no smaller than $-6.$ But before we conclude that $-6$ is the minimum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(\mathbf{x}) = -6.$

:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{2t}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}2-2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0 \\ 1{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{2t}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=1,$ and $a+b=1.$

Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ a\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ a\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-2t}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-2.$*
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-1+2 & -1 \\ 1 & -3+2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}-{w}_{2} &=1 \\ {w}_{1}-{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Note that the first equation is the same as the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}={w}_{2}+1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=1,$ and therefore

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-2t}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=1,b=1,$ and $a+b=2.$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 9 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 9 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2-1 & 9 \\ -1 & 4-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3 & 9 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3{w}_{1}+9{w}_{2} &=3 \\ -1{w}_{1}+3{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=3{w}_{2}-1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{t}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=3,b=-1,$ and $a+b=2.$

:question/problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =4$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}4-4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4-4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+2{w}_{2} &=1 \\ 0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$  we get

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{4t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}{e}^{4t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ \frac{{c}_{2}}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ \frac{{c}_{2}}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$  we get

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{6}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{6}\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ -\frac{{c}_{2}}{6}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ -\frac{{c}_{2}}{6}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

:question/problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{bmatrix}x(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{bmatrix}.$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-7+1 & -4 \\ 9 & 5+1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6{w}_{1}-4{w}_{2} &=-2 \\ 9{w}_{1}+6{w}_{2} &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3},$ and therefore

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-t}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+5(\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-t}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ 15\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(1-10t){e}^{-t} \\ (1+15t){e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}10 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =7.$*
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}10 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =7$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -9 & -3\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}10-7 & 1 \\ -9 & 4-7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -9 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{w}_{1}+{w}_{2} &=-1 \\ -9{w}_{1}-3{w}_{2} &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{{w}_{2}}{3}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3},$ and therefore

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{7t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{7t}+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{7t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}-{c}_{1}-\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-{c}_{1}-\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-3\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{7t}-3\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{7t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(1+3t){e}^{7t} \\ -9t{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-2+2 & -1 \\ 0 & -2+2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}-1{w}_{2}=1 \\ 0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=-1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$  we get

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ -{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ -{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(1+t){e}^{-2t} \\ -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =5$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}5-5 & 0 \\ -1 & 5-5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ -1{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{5t}. \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{5t} \\ (2+t){e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{w}_{1}=-1-{w}_{2}.

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

:question/problem:
If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ invertible matrix, then which of the following could be the characteristic equation of $A?$

I. $\lambda (\lambda +2)(\lambda -1)=0$

II. ${\lambda }^{3}+3{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +4=0$

III. ${\lambda }^{3}-5{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda =0$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is invertible, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $0$ can't be an eigenvalue of $A.$ As a result, $\lambda =0$ should not be a solution to the corresponding characteristic equation. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given equations in turn.

- Equation I **cannot** be the characteristic equation of $A$ since $\lambda =0$ is a root of the equation.

- Equation II could be the characteristic equation of $A.$ Indeed, $\lambda =0$ is not a root of the equation.

- Equation III **cannot** be the characteristic equation of $A$ since $\lambda =0$ is a root of the equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

:question/problem:
A matrix $A$ has the characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{3}-{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda =0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\lambda =3$ is a root of the characteristic equation
- **II.** $\lambda =0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$
- **III.** $A$ is invertible
:question/worked-solution:
The invertible matrix theorem in terms of eigenvectors states the following:

*The square matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A.$*

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, substituting $\lambda =3$ into the equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{3}-{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda  & =0 \\ (3)^{3}-(3)^{2}-6(3) & =0 \\ 27-9-18 & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $\lambda =0$ is a root of the characteristic equation. As a result, $\lambda =0$ is an eigenvalue of $A.$

- Statement III is false. Since $\lambda =0$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ according to the invertible matrix theorem, $A$ is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

- **III.** $\lambda =-2$ is an eigenvalue of $A$
:question/worked-solution:
Given a $3\times 3$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=3=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)={0} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $M$ has $3$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(M)+\text{nullity}(M)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A+2I) & =3-\text{nullity}(A+2I) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statements II is true. By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)\ne 0,$ we obtain that $A+2I$ must be singular.

- Statement III is true. Notice that if $M=A+2I$ is singular, then $(A+2I)x=0$ has nonzero solutions which will be eigenvectors of $A.$ As a result, $\lambda =-2$ is an eigenvalue of $A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:question/problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & a & ∗ \\ 2 & b & ∗ \\ 1 & c & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $a+b.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(3)
$$

So, we have

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =1,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =3.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(1) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(3) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =1,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have ${x}_{2}=-7+2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+(-7+2{x}_{3})=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5-2{x}_{3} \\ -7+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=0,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a+b=5+(-7)=-2.$

:question/worked-solution:

$$
J={J}_{2}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)
$$

So, we have

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =-2,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =1.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-2) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(1) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$ 

Now, computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 0 \\ 11 & 8 & 1\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 11 & 8 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 11 & 8 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-11){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+({x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{-1}{1}=-1.$

$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{c}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(4)
$$

So, we have

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =-2,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =4.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-2) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(4) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$ 

Now, computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 19 & 63 \\ 0 & 1 & 9 \\ 0 & -1 & -5\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 19 & 63 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 19 & 63 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -3 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & 19 & 63 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have ${x}_{2}=-3{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
6{x}_{1}+19(-3{x}_{3})+63{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=-1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{c}=\frac{3}{-1}=-3.$

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =3,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =-1.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(3) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(-1) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda =3.$ 

Now, computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ -19 & -15 & -1\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -19 & -15 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -19 & -15 & -4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-19){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}-({x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{c}=\frac{1}{1}=1.$

$$
J={J}_{2}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-1)
$$

So, we have

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =4,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =-1.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(4) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(-1) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =4,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-4I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 & 1 \\ -15 & -1 & -15 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ -15 & -5 & -15 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-4I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -15 & -5 & -15 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+15{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & -15 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the first and second equation, we have ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}-1$ and ${x}_{2}=3,$ respectively.

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{3}-1 \\ 3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=0,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, $a+c=-1+0=-1.$
